subject: Accounting
title: Compound Journal Entries
description: A 60-second lesson on Compound Journal Entries.

hook.text: A customer pays $500 in cash and $500 by credit card for a $1,000 purchase. That's three accounts in one entry.

buildup.text: Most entries have one debit and one credit. Compound entries involve two or more of each.

discovery.text: The rule still applies: total debits must equal total credits, no matter how many accounts are involved.

twist.text: Complex transactions like payroll can touch a dozen accounts in a single compound entry.

climax.text: Compound entries keep the books clean—one entry captures the full economic reality of the transaction.

punchline.text: More accounts, same rule: debits must equal credits.

quiz.question: What makes a journal entry compound?
options: It involves more than two accounts

details.summary: Compound journal entries involve more than two accounts in a single transaction—unlike simple entries that have just one debit and one credit. This topic explains when compound entries are needed and how to record them correctly.
details.whyItMatters: Many real business transactions affect more than two accounts simultaneously. Understanding compound entries is essential for accurately recording complex transactions like payroll or asset purchases with trade-ins.
takeaways: A compound entry has multiple debits, multiple credits, or both in one journal entry
Total debits must still equal total credits in every compound entry
Payroll journal entries are the most common example of compound entries in practice

faq.question: What is a compound journal entry?
faq.answer: A compound journal entry records a transaction that affects three or more accounts. For example, a payroll entry might debit Salary Expense and Payroll Tax Expense while crediting Cash, Tax Payable, and Benefits Payable—all in one entry.

faq.question: When do you use compound journal entries instead of simple ones?
faq.answer: Compound entries are used whenever a transaction naturally involves more than two accounts—such as recording a sale with sales tax, making payroll with deductions, or purchasing an asset with a partial cash payment and a loan for the balance.
